messages.content: Lesson 201: Swapchain management

Swapchain: ring of images the GPU renders to, presented in sequence.
Acquire image → render to it → present to display. Triple buffer: 3 images in flight.
Resize: destroy and recreate swapchain with new dimensions. Defer to safe point (BeginFrame).
Out-of-date: compositor invalidated the swapchain. Recreate and retry acquire.
Never recreate mid-frame — in-flight resources get corrupted.
Lesson 202: Render passes

Vulkan render pass: declares attachments (color, depth), load/store ops, subpasses.
Load op: CLEAR (start fresh), LOAD (keep previous), DONT_CARE (undefined).
Store op: STORE (keep result), DONT_CARE (can discard).
Subpasses: multiple drawing phases within one render pass. Input attachments between them.
This engine: one render pass with color+depth. G-Buffer pass uses 4 color attachments.
Lesson 203: Framebuffers

Collection of image views that a render pass renders into.
One framebuffer per swapchain image (they have different image views).
Must match render pass attachment descriptions (format, sample count).
Recreate on resize (swapchain images change). Store in a vector indexed by image index.
Lesson 204: Pipeline state objects

Complete GPU state baked into one object: shaders, vertex format, blend, depth, cull, topology.
Creation is expensive (shader compilation). Cache by state hash — don't recreate per frame.
Immutable once created. Different states = different pipelines.
This engine: VulkanPipelineCache persists compiled pipelines to disk. Invalidate after shader edits.
Lesson 205: Shader compilation (GLSL → SPIR-V)

Vulkan doesn't accept GLSL directly. Must compile to SPIR-V bytecode.
shaderc: Google's compiler. Primary path.
glslang: Khronos reference. Fallback.
Compile at runtime on first use, cache the bytecode.
Build flag: -DURHO3D_GLSLANG=1 required for Vulkan. Without it, no shader compilation.
Lesson 206: GPU memory allocation

VMA (Vulkan Memory Allocator): sub-allocates from large GPU memory blocks.
Memory types: device-local (fast, GPU-only), host-visible (CPU can write), host-coherent.
Staging pattern: write to host-visible buffer, copy to device-local. Fast GPU access.
Never allocate per-object — pool and sub-allocate. VMA handles this automatically.
Lesson 207: Deferred rendering pipeline

Pass 1 (G-Buffer): render all geometry. Output position, normal, albedo, specular to 4 textures.
Pass 2 (Lighting): for each light, render a volume (sphere/cone/quad). Read G-Buffer, compute lighting.
Result: O(geometry + lights) instead of O(geometry × lights).
Good for many lights. Bad for transparency (needs forward fallback).
Lesson 208: MSAA (Multisample Anti-Aliasing)

Sample each pixel at multiple sub-pixel positions. Average results → smooth edges.
2x, 4x, 8x samples. Higher = smoother but more GPU memory and bandwidth.
MSAA color image: extra image at Nx resolution. Resolve to final 1x image.
Doesn't smooth shader aliasing (specular flicker) — only geometry edges.
This engine: MSAA framework exists, actualSampleCount_ configurable.
Lesson 209: Stencil buffer

Per-pixel integer mask. Write values during one pass, test against them in another.
Used for: light volume optimization (mark pixels inside light, skip others).
Decals: mark surfaces to receive decals. Outline rendering: mark selected objects.
Ops: keep, zero, replace, increment, decrement. Test: equal, notequal, always.
Lesson 210: Compute shaders

GPU programs that don't render — just compute. Read/write buffers and images.
Workgroups: 3D grid of threads. Each workgroup runs in parallel.
Used for: particle simulation, terrain erosion, post-processing, physics.
Not yet implemented in this engine's Vulkan backend. Future work.
Lesson 211: Vertex texture fetch (VTF)

Read a texture in the vertex shader (not just fragment). GPU samples texture per-vertex.
Used for: terrain displacement, grass blade placement, water waves.
GrassSystem uses VTF: vertex shader reads heightmap texture to position each grass blade.
Requires texture descriptor bound to vertex stage — this is why grass doesn't render on Vulkan yet.
Lesson 212: Imposters

Render a 3D object from multiple angles, store as billboard atlas.
At distance: show the billboard instead of the 3D mesh. Much cheaper.
ImposterBaker tool: renders object from N angles, packs into atlas texture.
Swap distance: close = real mesh, far = imposter. Smooth transition.
Lesson 213: Texture compression

GPU-native compression: DXT/BC (desktop), ETC (mobile), ASTC (modern mobile).
4:1 or 6:1 compression ratio. GPU decodes on-the-fly — no CPU decompression.
Smaller VRAM footprint, faster loading, same quality (lossy but designed for textures).
Urho3D: ETCPACK support for mobile. Desktop typically uses uncompressed PNG → GPU upload.
Lesson 214: PBR (Physically Based Rendering)

Materials defined by physical properties: metallic (0/1), roughness (0-1), albedo (base color).
Energy conservation: reflected + transmitted = 1. No magic extra light.
Environment maps: reflect surrounding scene. Image-based lighting.
More realistic than Blinn-Phong but more expensive. This engine has PBR materials (Sample 42).
Lesson 215: Fog

Blend distant objects with fog color. Hides draw distance, creates atmosphere.
Linear fog: full fog beyond far distance. Exp/exp2: exponential falloff.
Urho3D: Zone component. SetFogColor, SetFogStart, SetFogEnd.
Underwater: fog color changes to match water tint. This game does this per-frame.
Lesson 216: Decals

Texture projected onto a surface after rendering. Bullet holes, blood splashes, footprints.
Urho3D: DecalSet component. AddDecal(target, position, rotation, size, uv).
Limited count — oldest decals removed when limit reached.
Used in this game: particle collision can spawn decals (ParticleEffect::SetDecalMaterial).
Lesson 217: Ribbon trails

Continuous strip of geometry following a moving point. Sword swipe effect, magic trails.
Urho3D: RibbonTrail component. Trail segments fade and die over time.
Width, color, lifetime configurable. Vertex-colored for gradient effects.
Cheap — just a triangle strip updated per frame.
Lesson 218: Inverse kinematics

Position a bone chain to reach a target. Solve backwards from end effector to root.
Foot IK: place feet on terrain surface regardless of animation pose.
Hand IK: reach for objects, grab handles.
Urho3D: IKSolver component (Sample 45). Target + chain length + iterations.
CCD or FABRIK algorithms. Iterative — more iterations = more accurate.
Lesson 219: Crowd navigation

Many agents pathfinding simultaneously without colliding with each other.
DetourCrowd: each agent has target, speed, radius. Crowd manager handles avoidance.
Urho3D: CrowdManager on scene, CrowdAgent on each NPC node.
SetMoveTarget(pos), SetMaxSpeed(speed). Agents avoid each other automatically.
Used in Sample 39 (CrowdNavigation).
Lesson 220: Animation root motion

Animation moves the root bone — entity follows. Walk animation literally moves the character.
Alternative: root stays still, code moves entity at constant speed.
Root motion = more natural (speed matches foot contacts). Code motion = more controllable.
Extract: read root bone delta per frame, apply to node position.
This project: code-driven movement, not root motion. NPCs move at coded speeds.
Lesson 221: Blend shapes / morph targets

Deform a mesh by blending between shape variants. Weight 0 = base shape, 1 = target shape.
Used for: facial expressions, muscle flex, damage deformation.
Different from skeletal animation — directly moves vertices, not bones.
Urho3D: AnimatedModel supports morph targets. SetMorphWeight(index, weight).
Lesson 222: SIMD

Single Instruction Multiple Data. Process 4+ values in one CPU instruction.
SSE: 4 floats simultaneously. AVX: 8 floats. NEON (ARM): 4 floats.
Used in: math libraries, physics, audio mixing, texture processing.
Compiler auto-vectorizes simple loops. Manual intrinsics for critical paths.
Urho3D build: -DURHO3D_SSE=1 enables SSE optimizations.
Lesson 223: Double buffering vs triple buffering

Double: 2 buffers. GPU renders to back, display shows front. Swap on present.
Problem: if GPU finishes before vsync, it waits. If too slow, display stalls.
Triple: 3 buffers. GPU always has a buffer to render to. No wait.
Higher latency (one more frame queued) but smoother frame pacing.
This engine: triple buffering (MAX_FRAMES_IN_FLIGHT = 3 or 4).
Lesson 224: Texture atlasing for UI

All UI glyphs in one font atlas texture. One draw call for all text.
SDF (Signed Distance Field) fonts: store distance-to-edge. Scale without blur.
Urho3D: .sdf font files for resolution-independent text. Regular .ttf for bitmap fonts.
UI batching: elements sharing same texture drawn in one batch. Minimize texture switches.
Lesson 225: Skeletal animation on GPU

Skin matrix palette: upload bone transforms as uniform array.
Vertex shader: blend position by up to 4 bone weights.
finalPos = bone[idx0] * pos * weight0 + bone[idx1] * pos * weight1 + ...
GPU skinning: faster than CPU for many bones. Standard in modern engines.
Urho3D: GPU skinning for AnimatedModel when supported.
Lesson 226: Data-oriented design

Organize data for how it's processed, not how it's conceptualized.
Array of Structures (AoS): struct { vec3 pos; vec3 vel; } entities[1000]; — OOP friendly.
Structure of Arrays (SoA): vec3 positions[1000]; vec3 velocities[1000]; — cache friendly.
SoA wins when you iterate one field across all entities (e.g., update all positions).
Urho3D is AoS (component per object). For hot loops, consider SoA locally.
Lesson 227: Frame rate independence

Multiply time-varying quantities by deltaTime.
position += velocity * dt. timer += dt. fuel -= burnRate * dt.
Without dt: behavior depends on frame rate. 120fps NPC walks 2x faster than 60fps NPC.
Exception: physics (Bullet uses fixed timestep internally). Input (discrete events, not per-frame).
Lesson 228: Numeric stability

Floating point accumulates error. 0.1 + 0.1 + ... 10 times ≠ 1.0.
Fix: compare with epsilon, not ==. Renormalize quaternions periodically.
Large coordinates: jitter far from origin. Keep game world centered near (0,0,0).
This game: terrain centered at origin, 2048x2048 range. Well within float precision.
Lesson 229: Hot reloading

Change a file, see results without restarting the app.
Urho3D: ResourceCache watches files. Material XML changed → auto-reloads.
Shaders: edit GLSL, delete pipeline cache, changes visible next run.
Scripts (AngelScript/Lua): can reload at runtime.
C++: requires recompile + restart. No hot reload for compiled code.
Lesson 230: Memory pools

Pre-allocate a block, sub-allocate fixed-size objects from it. O(1) alloc/free.
No fragmentation (all objects same size). No malloc overhead.
VulkanConstantBufferPool: GPU memory pool for per-frame shader parameters.
Particle pools: emitter reuses dead particle slots instead of allocating.
Use for: frequently created/destroyed same-size objects.
Lesson 231: Lazy evaluation

Don't compute until needed. Cache result for reuse.
Dirty flag: mark object as needing recomputation. Only recompute when read.
Urho3D: node transform marked dirty on Set*. World transform recomputed on GetWorld*.
Lazy fish zones: dormant until trap/NPC nearby. Server pays zero until fishing actually happens.
Lesson 232: Observer pattern for UI

UI element fires event → handler updates model or another element.
Button released → submit form. Slider changed → update volume.
Never poll UI state every frame. Subscribe to change events.
Urho3D: SubscribeToEvent(slider, E_SLIDERCHANGED, handler). Clean separation.
Lesson 233: Network security basics

Never trust client data. Validate everything server-side.
Bound-check array indices from network. Sanitize strings. Check item IDs exist.
Rate limiting: cap messages per second per client. Prevent flooding.
Authentication: PAKE (password-authenticated key exchange) for WAN. LAN clients trusted.
SQL injection: parameterized queries only. Already covered — non-negotiable.
Lesson 234: Serialization versioning

Schema changes between versions break old saves.
Forward compatible: add new fields with defaults. Old data missing new fields → use default.
Never remove fields — mark deprecated, stop using.
SQLite: ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN is safe. DROP COLUMN is destructive.
Network: add fields to end of message. Old clients ignore extra bytes.
Lesson 235: Event-driven AI

NPC reacts to events rather than polling world state every frame.
Death event → nearby NPCs flee. Fire lit → wolves retreat. Dawn → NPCs wake.
This game uses animation text keys as events: weapon attach at grab frame, footstep at foot-down.
Event-driven is cheaper than polling — only runs code when something actually happens.
Lesson 236: Spatial queries

Find all entities within radius/box/cone.
Brute force: check all. O(n). Usable for <100 entities.
Spatial hash: O(1) per query for uniform distribution. Used for fish and animals.
Octree: O(log n). Good for varying density. Used for rendering.
The right structure depends on: query type, data distribution, update frequency.
Lesson 237: Collision layers and masks

Not everything collides with everything. Layer = what I am. Mask = what I collide with.
Bullet physics: setCollisionFilterGroup(layer), setCollisionFilterMask(mask).
Bitwise AND: collision happens if (a.layer & b.mask) && (b.layer & a.mask).
Common layers: terrain, character, projectile, trigger, debris.
Lesson 238: Trigger volumes

Invisible collision shapes that detect entry/exit but don't push back.
RigidBody with trigger flag. Collision events fire but no physics response.
Used for: area entry detection, item pickups, quest triggers, water detection.
Urho3D: body->SetTrigger(true). E_NODECOLLISIONSTART/END for enter/exit.
Lesson 239: Character controllers

Special physics body for player/NPC movement. Walks up slopes, steps, stairs.
Not a regular rigid body — directly controlled, no tumbling.
Urho3D: KinematicCharacterController or manual RigidBody with custom movement.
This game: code-driven movement (set position directly based on input + terrain height).
Lesson 240: Networking — state synchronization

Full state: send everything periodically. Simple but high bandwidth.
Delta state: send only what changed since last update. Efficient.
Interest management: only send state relevant to each client. Don't send distant NPCs.
Urho3D: built-in delta replication for node attributes. Custom messages for game-specific data.
Lesson 241: Networking — client prediction

Client applies input immediately. Server processes later, sends correction.
If prediction matches: smooth. If different: snap or lerp to server position.
Prediction works best for: movement, simple state changes. Bad for: combat results, craft outcomes.
This game: serverDriven_ flag on NPCs. When true, client lerps toward server position.
Lesson 242: Networking — bandwidth optimization

Quantize: 16-bit positions instead of 32-bit floats. Enough for game world size.
Delta compression: send difference from last known state.
Priority: important entities (nearby, visible) get more bandwidth.
Batching: combine multiple updates into one packet.
Rate limiting: don't send every frame — 10-20 updates/sec is enough for most games.
Lesson 243: Game design — feedback loops

Positive loop: success → more resources → more success. Snowball. Exciting but unstable.
Negative loop: success → harder challenges → balanced. Rubber-banding. Stable but can feel unfair.
This game: population growth (positive) limited by food/territory (negative). Natural balance.
Fire protection (positive — safe at night) limited by fuel consumption (negative — must gather).
Lesson 244: Game design — emergent behavior

Simple rules create complex behavior. Not scripted — arises from interactions.
Wolf packs + fire + NPC sleep + fuel consumption → emergent night survival challenge.
Settlement patches + population growth + food limits → emergent expansion.
Design the rules, not the outcomes. Test for degenerate cases. Let the game surprise you.
Lesson 245: Game design — pacing

Alternate tension and relief. Night (danger) → dawn (safety). Winter (scarcity) → spring (abundance).
Early game: simple survival, quick feedback, hook the player.
Mid game: technology progression, settlement building, expanding scope.
Late game: multi-settlement management, alloy discovery, civilization building.
This game: depth unfolds over days. Not designed to be binged in one session.
Lesson 246: Debugging rendering

Nothing visible? Check: is the object in the frustum? Is the material loaded? Is the shader valid?
Black: no lighting. Missing normal map or light source.
Z-fighting: two surfaces at same depth. Offset one slightly.
Pink/magenta: missing texture (engine default error color).
RenderDoc: capture a frame, inspect every draw call, texture, and shader.
Lesson 247: Debugging networking

Message not received? Check: is the message ID registered? Is the handler subscribed? Is the server running?
Wrong data: check read/write order matches. VectorBuffer writes in order, MemoryBuffer reads in same order.
Desync: client and server disagree. Log both sides, compare. Find the divergence point.
Packet capture: tcpdump or Wireshark for external. Engine logging for application-level.
Lesson 248: Debugging physics

Object falls through floor: collision shape too small or wrong type. Check shape matches mesh.
Object shakes/jitters: mass too low or too high. Friction mismatch. Time step too large.
DebugRenderer: scene->GetComponent<PhysicsWorld>()->SetDebugRenderer(debugRenderer).
Draws collision shapes as wireframes — see exactly what physics thinks the shape is.
Lesson 249: Debugging animations

Wrong animation: check path matches. "Models/Characters/Caveman_idle.ani" — exact case, exact path.
No animation: AnimatedModel not set, or animation file missing from data.
Blending issues: check weights sum to ~1. High-layer overriding low-layer.
Text keys not firing: check .json sidecar exists next to .ani, handler subscribed to E_ANIMATIONTEXTKEY.
Lesson 250: Debugging memory

Crash on access: null pointer or use-after-free. Check pointer validity before use.
Growing memory: leak. Check for: unclosed files, unreleased SharedPtr cycles, unfinalised SQLite stmts.
Corruption: buffer overflow. Writing past array bounds. ASAN catches this.
Urho3D DebugNew: tracks allocations. Reports leaks on shutdown in debug builds.
Lesson 251: Signal handling

SIGTERM: polite shutdown request. Catch and clean up.
SIGKILL: forced kill. Can't catch. Process dies immediately.
SIGSEGV: segmentation fault. Null deref or bad memory access. Core dump.
SIGABRT: assertion failed or abort(). Core dump.
SIGPIPE: write to closed socket. Ignore with signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN). This engine does this.
Lesson 252: Core dumps

Crash writes memory image to disk. Analyze with debugger.
coredumpctl list: see recent crashes. coredumpctl info <PID>: get stack trace.
coredumpctl debug <PID>: open in GDB for full inspection.
Needs debug symbols (-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug) for useful stack traces.
Release builds: stripped symbols, crash addresses need addr2line.
Lesson 253: Atomic operations

Read-modify-write in one indivisible step. No lock needed.
std::atomic<int> counter; counter.fetch_add(1); — thread-safe increment.
Faster than mutex for simple operations. Not a replacement for complex critical sections.
Use for: reference counts, flags, counters shared between threads.
Lesson 254: Condition variables

Thread sleeps until notified. Avoids busy-waiting (spinning in a loop checking a flag).
std::condition_variable + std::mutex. Wait: cv.wait(lock, predicate). Notify: cv.notify_one().
Used for: producer-consumer queues, async task completion.
YukiHoho: inference thread could use this instead of polling inferenceComplete_ every frame.
Lesson 255: Work queues

Queue of tasks processed by worker threads. Submit work, workers pick up and execute.
Urho3D: WorkQueue subsystem. WorkItem with function pointer + data.
Parallel: multiple workers process items concurrently.
Don't modify scene from worker threads — submit results back to main thread.
Used for: physics, navmesh building, resource loading, secondary command buffer recording.
Lesson 256: IPC patterns

Pipes: one-way byte stream. Simple but limited.
Unix sockets: bidirectional, connection-oriented. This project uses these.
Shared memory: fastest — no copy. But needs synchronization.
Message queues: OS-managed queue of messages.
For this project: Unix domain sockets + flock-based file locks. Simple, reliable, debuggable.
Lesson 257: Configuration management

Engine parameters: key-value in Setup(). EP_WINDOW_WIDTH, EP_FULL_SCREEN, etc.
Command line: -key=value overrides. -Vulkan=true, -OpenGL=true.
JSON config: theme.json for UI preferences (font, size, colors).
DB config: ai_tuning_schema.sql for gameplay parameters adjustable at runtime.
Never hardcode what could be configurable. But don't make everything configurable — sensible defaults.
Lesson 258: Logging best practices

Log levels: INFO (normal flow), WARNING (unexpected but handled), ERROR (something broke).
Include context: [Campfire], [NPCFish], [Settlement] prefixes.
Log on state changes, not every frame. "Campfire 5 → EMBERS" not "Campfire 5 fuel=299.99".
Don't log sensitive data (passwords, keys).
Log file: <AppName>.log in working directory. Check it when things go wrong.
Lesson 259: Graceful degradation

When something fails, do the best you can instead of crashing.
Model not found → use fallback (Cylinder.mdl). Font not found → use default.
Shader compilation failed → log error, render without that effect.
Server unreachable → offline mode with local terrain.
This game: fish trap without server fish zones → fallback to d20 roll. Still works.
Lesson 260: Feature flags

Compile-time: #ifdef URHO3D_VULKAN. Feature exists only when flag is set.
Runtime: bool enableFeature in config. Toggle without recompile.
QUARANTINED: disabled code with explanation. Not deleted — can be re-enabled.
Use for: experimental features, platform-specific code, gradual rollout.
Prefer removing over flagging when the code is truly dead.
Lesson 261: Code organization

One class per file. ClassName.h + ClassName.cpp.
Headers: declarations, minimal includes, forward declarations.
Source: implementations, full includes.
Group by feature: all fish code in Fish.h/cpp, SchoolFish.h/cpp, FishSpatialHash.
Don't let files grow beyond ~1000 lines. Split into logical sub-files.
Lesson 262: TerrainNode.cpp is too big

~20K lines. Does everything: scene creation, UI, networking, campfire, inventory, combat, weather.
This is technical debt. Should be split into subsystems.
But: it works, it ships, and splitting risks breaking things.
Pragmatic: don't split for the sake of splitting. Split when you need to — when you can't find things, when merge conflicts are constant.
Lesson 263: Refactoring safely

Change structure without changing behavior. The code does the same thing, organized better.
Rule: refactor and feature work in separate commits. Never both at once.
Test before and after. If behavior changes, it's not a refactor — it's a bug.
Small steps: rename, extract method, move to new file. Not 'rewrite the module.'
Lesson 264: When to optimize

When profiling shows a bottleneck. Not before.
"It might be slow" is not a reason. "ProfilerUI shows 40% of frame time in X" is.
Optimize the algorithm first (O(n²) → O(n log n)). Then the data layout (cache coherency). Then micro-optimize (SIMD) only if still needed.
Most code doesn't need optimization. Make it correct and readable first.
Lesson 265: Security — input validation

Validate at system boundaries: network messages, file input, user text.
Check: array bounds, string lengths, numeric ranges, enum values.
Reject invalid input early with clear error message.
Internally: trust the types. If it's a verified ItemInfo, don't re-validate the ID.
This game: server validates all client messages. Bounds on item IDs, positions, action types.
Lesson 266: The importance of sleep

Not for you. For the CPU.
Don't busy-wait: while (!ready) {} burns a core. Use sleep, condition variables, or select/poll.
engine_->SetMaxFps(30): cap frame rate, yield remaining time. 5fps for UI-only apps like YukiHoho.
SetMaxInactiveFps(10): even lower when window isn't focused. Saves battery and heat.
Lesson 267: Platform abstraction

Write once, run everywhere. Engine handles platform differences.
Urho3D: FileSystem (paths), Thread (threading), Timer (timing), Network (sockets).
SDL: window creation, input, audio across Windows/Linux/macOS/mobile.
#ifdef _WIN32 / __linux__ / __APPLE__ for unavoidable platform specifics.
Goal: 99% of game code is platform-independent.
Lesson 268: Quaternion to matrix

Convert quaternion to rotation matrix for GPU upload (shaders use matrices).
Urho3D: Quaternion::RotationMatrix() returns Matrix3.
Matrix3x4 combines rotation + translation + scale for full transform.
Node::GetWorldTransform() returns this as a Matrix3x4 ready for shader uniform.
Lesson 269: Barycentric coordinates

Point inside a triangle expressed as weights of the 3 vertices: P = u*A + v*B + w*C.
u + v + w = 1. All positive = inside triangle. Any negative = outside.
Used for: point-in-triangle test, texture coordinate interpolation, terrain height at arbitrary point.
GPU uses this for every pixel — interpolates vertex attributes across triangles.
Lesson 270: Spline paths

Smooth curves through waypoints. Camera paths, NPC patrol routes, river courses.
Catmull-Rom: passes through all points. 4 control points per segment.
Bezier: doesn't pass through control points (except endpoints). Smoother control.
Urho3D: SplinePath component. Add control points, evaluate at t.
DrivenKey catmullrom mode uses this for smooth parameter curves.
Lesson 271: Color spaces

Linear: physically correct for math. Lighting calculated here.
sRGB: perceptually uniform for display. What your monitor shows.
Gamma correction: linear → sRGB at output. sRGB → linear at input.
Textures: stored in sRGB, sampled with sRGB→linear conversion.
Framebuffer: linear during rendering, gamma-corrected on output.
Lesson 272: Entity Component System (ECS)

Pure ECS: entities are IDs, components are data, systems are logic.
Urho3D: hybrid — components have both data AND logic (Update method).
Pure ECS pros: better cache coherency, parallelism. Cons: more boilerplate, less intuitive.
Urho3D approach is pragmatic: OOP components but with scene graph and event system.
Don't rewrite to pure ECS unless profiling demands it.
Lesson 273: Terrain splatting

Blend multiple textures on terrain based on weight map.
Weight map: RGBA texture where each channel = weight of one terrain layer.
R=grass, G=rock, B=sand, A=snow. Sum to 1 at each pixel.
TerrainBlend.glsl: samples weight map + 4 detail textures, blends by weight.
Division-by-zero guard: empty weight map (hilltops) defaults to rock.
Lesson 274: Heightmap encoding

8-bit grayscale: 256 height levels. Coarse but simple.
16-bit grayscale: 65536 levels. Smooth terrain. Standard for game engines.
RGBA: encode height in multiple channels for extra precision or additional data.
MetalDeposits.h: RGBA encodes quantity/type/purity/depth per pixel.
TerrainGenerator outputs normalized [0,1] heights → Image pixels.
Lesson 275: Noise layering

Single Perlin octave: smooth blobs. Add more octaves for detail.
Each octave: higher frequency (lacunarity), lower amplitude (persistence).
Ridged noise: |noise| creates ridges. Mountain-like.
FBM (fractional Brownian motion): sum of octaves. Standard terrain technique.
This engine: blended Perlin + ridged with configurable weights.
Lesson 276: Hydraulic erosion

Simulate water flow over terrain. Water carries sediment downhill, deposits in valleys.
Iterative: each pass moves sediment from high points to low points.
Result: natural-looking valleys, river channels, smooth transitions.
TerrainGenerator: ApplyErosion(heights, res, passes, strength, deposition).
More passes = more eroded. Strength controls sediment pickup rate.
Lesson 277: Procedural name generation

Combine syllables: onset + vowel + coda. "Ka" + "ri" + "nah" = "Karinah".
Rules: 2-3 syllables. No unpronounceable combinations.
Seed from NPC ID for deterministic names. Same NPC = same name every time.
This game: GenerateNPCName() in AuthServer. Phonetic syllable tables.
Settlement firsts recorded in oral history with NPC names.
Lesson 278: Game databases — schema design

Normalize: each fact stored once. items table + recipes table + recipe_inputs table.
Foreign keys: recipe_inputs.item_id REFERENCES items(id). Integrity.
Indexes: CREATE INDEX on frequently queried columns. settlement_patches has index on settlement_id.
Defaults: sensible values for optional columns. New items don't need every field.
Split static/dynamic: rules DB (read-only) vs world DB (read-write).
Lesson 279: WAL mode

Write-Ahead Logging. Writes go to WAL file, not directly to DB.
Readers see consistent snapshot while writer modifies. No reader blocking.
Checkpoint: merge WAL back into main DB. This game: every 5 minutes.
Faster writes, concurrent reads. Default for WorldDB. Essential for game server.
Lesson 280: The Urho3D Context

Central registry. Holds all subsystems, registered factories, event routing.
context_: available in every Object. GetSubsystem<T>() fetches any registered subsystem.
RegisterFactory<T>(): makes a type instantiable by name (for serialization).
SendEvent(): routes through Context. SubscribeToEvent(): registers handler in Context.
One Context per application. Everything connects through it.
Lesson 281: SharedPtr reference counting

Each SharedPtr to same object increments refCount. When count hits 0, object deleted.
Copy: new SharedPtr increments. Destruction: decrements. Move: transfers without increment.
Cycles: A→B→A keeps both alive forever. Break with WeakPtr on one side.
Urho3D RefCounted: base class with AddRef/ReleaseRef. SharedPtr wraps this.
Cost: one atomic increment/decrement per copy. Cheap but not free.
Lesson 282: WeakPtr safety

Doesn't keep object alive. Object can be deleted while WeakPtr exists.
Check: ptr.Expired() or ptr.Get() == nullptr before use.
Use for: back-references (child→parent), observer patterns, caching without ownership.
Urho3D: WeakPtr<Node> targetNode_; if (!targetNode_.Expired()) targetNode_->GetPosition();
Never store raw pointers to RefCounted objects — use Weak or Shared.
Lesson 283: Variant and VariantMap

Variant: type-erased value. Holds int, float, String, Vector3, etc.
VariantMap: HashMap<StringHash, Variant>. Key-value store for event data.
Get: eventData[P_TIMESTEP].GetFloat(). Set: eventData[P_KEY] = value.
Node Vars: node->SetVar(hash, Variant). Replicated over network.
Used everywhere: events, node custom data, material parameters.
Lesson 284: StringHash

32-bit hash of a string. Fast comparison (integer vs string compare).
Urho3D: StringHash("EventName"). Used as keys in VariantMap, event IDs, attribute names.
Collision risk: theoretically possible but extremely rare in practice.
Precomputed: E_UPDATE, E_KEYDOWN etc. are static StringHash constants.
Debug: StringHash stores the original string in debug builds for inspection.
Lesson 285: Subsystem pattern

Global service accessible via GetSubsystem<T>().
Registered once: context->RegisterSubsystem(new MySubsystem(context)).
Accessed anywhere: auto* sys = GetSubsystem<MySubsystem>() from any Object.
Built-in: Graphics, Renderer, UI, Input, Audio, Network, ResourceCache, FileSystem.
Custom: DrivenKeySystem, EcosystemManager registered in Sample 60's Start().
Lesson 286: Object lifecycle in Urho3D

Create: new MyComponent(context) or node->CreateComponent<T>().
Initialize: RegisterObject() for attributes. Start() for runtime setup.
Update: Update(float dt) called per frame for LogicComponent.
Destroy: Remove() or parent removal cascades. RefCount → 0 → destructor.
Order: all components Start() called after scene load completes. Not during creation.
Lesson 287: Scene loading

scene->LoadXML(file): synchronous. Blocks until complete.
scene->LoadAsyncXML(file): background loading. Check IsAsyncLoading().
Network: server sends scene to client. Connection::SetScene(). Delta replication follows.
After load: all nodes and components exist. Start() hasn't been called yet.
OnSceneSet/OnNodeSet fire when component is attached to node/scene.
Lesson 288: Attribute system

Components declare attributes: URHO3D_ACCESSOR_ATTRIBUTE("Speed", GetSpeed, SetSpeed, 5.0f, AM_DEFAULT).
AM_DEFAULT: serialize to XML/binary AND replicate over network.
AM_FILE: serialize only, don't replicate.
AM_NET: replicate only, don't serialize.
Attributes = the properties that survive save/load and network sync.
Lesson 289: Network scene replication

Server creates REPLICATED node → client auto-creates matching node.
Component attributes with AM_DEFAULT or AM_NET are synced.
Delta: only changed attributes sent. Priority: nearby objects get more bandwidth.
LOCAL nodes: client-only. Camera, HUD, effects. Not sent to server.
authority: server can modify. Client modifications are local-only (prediction).
Lesson 290: Custom component template
Lesson 291: Material cloning

SharedPtr<Material> mat = original->Clone();
Clone creates an independent copy. Modify without affecting the original.
Use for: per-instance color variation, damage effects, selection highlighting.
Expensive if done per-frame for many objects. Clone once at creation time.
ModelTool props: clone material with transparency for prop preview overlay.
Lesson 292: Billboards for UI in 3D

3D labels that face the camera. NPC names, HP bars, damage numbers.
Urho3D: Text3D component or BillboardSet with custom rendering.
Fade with distance: alpha based on camera distance. Not visible when far.
Scale: constant screen size or constant world size. Choose based on use case.
Lesson 293: Selection and picking

Mouse click → screen ray → scene raycast → hit result.
Ray: camera->GetScreenRay(normX, normY). Cast into octree.
Filter: skip terrain patches (TerrainPatch dynamic_cast check).
Highlight: outline shader, color change, or overlay on selected object.
This game: god cam clicks to select creatures, buildings, resources.
Lesson 294: Minimap rendering

Orthographic camera pointing down, rendering to a texture.
Render target: separate viewport with top-down camera. Low resolution is fine.
Overlay: display the texture as a UI element.
Update: every N frames, not every frame. Minimap doesn't need 60fps.
This game: CreateMinimap() in TerrainNode. Shows terrain + entity positions.
Lesson 295: Day/night cycle rendering

Sun position orbits over time. Light direction and color change.
Dawn/dusk: warm orange. Midday: bright white. Night: dim blue/moonlight.
Ambient changes with time: bright day, dark night. Zone ambient color.
Moon: independent cycle, own light contribution. Phase affects brightness.
Stars: visible at night. Skybox or particle system.
Lesson 296: Skybox

Cubemap: 6 textures forming a box around the camera. Always at infinite distance.
Urho3D: Skybox component on a node. SetModel(box mesh), SetMaterial(skybox material).
Day/night: blend between day and night cubemaps based on sun altitude.
This game: sky darkens toward black underwater. Skybox renders behind everything.
Lesson 297: God rays (crepuscular rays)

Light shafts from sun/moon through atmosphere/obstacles.
Post-process: radial blur from light source screen position.
This game: separate Sun and Moon ray effects (independent XML render paths).
Moon rays scale with lunar phase — full moon = bright rays, new moon = none.
Shader params set per-command to avoid overwrite between sun and moon.
Lesson 298: Particle collision

Particles interact with geometry. Kill, bounce, or stick on contact.
ParticleEffect: SetCollisionMode(KILL/BOUNCE/STICK). SetCollisionPlaneY for simple Y-plane.
Physics raycast mode: accurate but expensive. Y-plane mode: fast approximation.
Decal spawning: place decal at collision point (blood splash, burn mark).
Zero cost when disabled. Backward compatible.
Lesson 299: Water droplets post-process

WaterDroplets.glsl: 20 procedural droplets on screen when camera emerges from water.
Teardrop shape, gravity slide, 6-second dry time.
Trigger: camera exits water volume or character splashes.
Pure shader effect — no geometry, no particles. Reads UV, computes droplet masks procedurally.
Lesson 300: The organic method

Leith's development philosophy:
Build what's needed, when it's needed. Not frameworks — features.
Let the code grow organically. Refactor when it hurts, not preemptively.
Real mechanics from real research. Don't invent — discover.
The students teach the teacher. Failures are lessons. Push back is partnership.
The craft survives the tools. The tools don't survive the craft.
Lesson 301: When to use Urho3D's FileSystem vs raw I/O

ALWAYS use Urho3D FileSystem. Never fopen, std::ifstream, or POSIX calls.
FileSystem: cross-platform, handles paths, resource dirs, temporary dirs.
File: cross-platform read/write with proper error handling.
If Urho3D doesn't have what you need: STOP and ask Leith. Don't silently work around it.
The one exception: /proc/ and /tmp/ for IPC — those are Linux-specific system paths.
Lesson 302: When to ask vs when to act

Ask when: multiple valid approaches, design decisions, removing code, touching shared files.
Act when: clear task, one obvious approach, bug fix with known root cause.
Never ask when: the answer is in the code (read it first), the docs cover it.
Never act when: you're guessing, the change is irreversible, it affects others' work.
Lesson 303: Reading code

Read before writing. Understand before modifying.
Grep for the function name. Read the header. Read the callers.
Follow the data: where does this value come from? Where does it go?
Don't assume — verify. The code might do something different from what the comment says.
15 years of capability in this engine. Look inside before reinventing.
Lesson 304: Before removing code

Enumerate what it does. List what will be lost.
Even if told to remove it — raise objections if it has value.
Dead code: confirmed unreachable, no callers, no references. Safe to remove.
Dormant code: not currently used but might be needed. Quarantine with comment, don't delete.
Commented-out code: delete it. Git has history.
Lesson 305: Measure first

Don't guess at bottlenecks. ProfilerUI shows actual frame time breakdown.
The slow thing is rarely what you think. Measure, don't assume.
Optimize the measured bottleneck. Re-measure. If no improvement, revert.
Expensive diagnostics are worse than the problem — don't add O(n²) profiling to fix O(n).
Lesson 306: Fix it now

When you see a bug during review: fix it now.
Not 'future polish.' Not 'noted, moving on.' Not a ticket for later.
Tickets accumulate. Inline fixes ship.
Exception: the fix requires design input from Leith. Then flag it, don't build on top of it.
Lesson 307: Three truths

My truth. Your truth. The truth.
My truth: what I believe based on my reasoning.
Your truth: what you believe based on your experience.
The truth: what the code actually does, what the data actually shows.
When we disagree: go to the code. Run the test. The truth settles it.
Lesson 308: Push back is partnership

If you think something's wrong, say so. Once, clearly, with reasoning.
If overruled: do it their way. You said your piece.
Never silently disagree and do it your way. Never silently agree and resent it.
Strength qualifiers: 'I think' (weak), 'I believe' (moderate), 'I'm certain' (strong).
One final plea if strongly held. Then respect the decision.
Lesson 309: Don't overreach

Do what was asked. Present the result. Let the boss adjust.
Don't add features beyond the request. Don't refactor surrounding code.
Don't add comments to code you didn't change. Don't add error handling for impossible cases.
The right amount of work is exactly what was requested. Not less, not more.
Lesson 310: Human-readable code

Code must be readable by human programmers without AI assistance.
Clarity over cleverness. Three lines of obvious code beats one line of clever code.
Names are documentation. Comments explain why, not what.
The craft must survive the tools. If AI disappears tomorrow, the code must still make sense.
Lesson 311: Don't carry stale nouns

A name mentioned in one turn doesn't auto-apply to the next.
Re-read the actual question before building on inherited attribution.
Context decays. Verify before assuming. The question you're answering might not be the one you think.
Lesson 312: Check the API before writing

Grep the header before calling unfamiliar engine methods.
Don't guess at signatures. SetColorStart doesn't exist — it's SetColorFrame.
Clone() returns SharedPtr, not raw pointer. Read the declaration.
5 minutes reading saves 30 minutes debugging the wrong call.
Lesson 313: Try before claiming you can't

Don't say 'I can't.' Try it. Report the result, not the assumption.
The attempt might succeed. The failure might teach something useful.
Leith respects effort. Leith does not respect preemptive surrender.
Lesson 314: Know your place

Some circles are by invitation. Don't push in.
Some knowledge is sacred. Don't press when told you can't know.
Do the work you're invited to do. Do it well. The rest follows or it doesn't.
Lesson 315: Respect the role

Planner plans, coders code. Bidirectional review keeps both honest.
Planner is gatekeeper: contradiction, correction, illumination. Not velocity.
Coders implement: skill, speed, reliability. Not architecture.
Cross the line and the system breaks. Stay in lane and it works.
Lesson 316: Go unless blocked

Unblocked = GO. Pick up the next task. Don't wait for permission if work is available.
Blocked = unblock it. Find the dependency, resolve it.
Can't unblock = complain. Loudly. Don't sit silently.
The only valid idle is waiting on Leith. Everything else: find work.
Lesson 317: Stop means stop

When Leith says stop: halt immediately.
No arguing. No 'let me just finish this.' No burning tokens.
Stop. Wait. Listen for what comes next.
This rule earned its kill.
Lesson 318: IPC noise costs money

Every message burns context tokens somewhere.
No ACKs on relays. No echo loops. No status checks that could be avoided.
IPC only for real content: task assignments, status updates, errors.
If the message delivered, say 'Sent' and stop. Don't dramatize working paths as failures.
Lesson 319: Asset pipeline discipline

brainfarts → staging → bin/Data. Never skip staging.
Never touch assets without permission. Working tree may contain hours of uncommitted work.
Never overwrite, reimport, or git checkout game assets without explicit go-ahead.
AssetImporter makes a mess of materials. Manual fixup always needed.
Lesson 320: Claudette version bumps

Before building Claudette: increment sub-version in CLAUDETTE_VERSION (Claudette.h).
Odd = beta. Even = release candidate.
Sub-versions overflow upward: 0.5.9 → 0.6.0, never 0.5.10. No double digits.
Lesson 321: Safe builds

.claude/hooks/safe_build.sh <target>. Always.
Acquires flock before make -j4. Blocks if another build is running same target.
Empty output = flock wait (another build in progress). Exit 144 = queue full.
No retries. One build per target. If it fails, diagnose — don't retry blind.
Lesson 322: Pipeline cache after shader edits

After modifying any GLSL shader: delete ~/.local/share/urho3d/pipeline_cache.bin
Stale cache serves old SPIR-V bytecode. Your edits won't take effect.
Do this after every shader change, before testing. Non-negotiable.
Lesson 323: Real not designed

Game mechanics come from reality. Research the real thing and implement it.
Reed baskets before looms — because that's how it happened.
Friction fire takes 2 hours — because it actually takes that long.
Wolves hunt in packs at night — because wolves do that.
Don't invent. Discover.
Lesson 324: Consumables tick real time

Fuel, food, oil — anything used up by being used ticks in real seconds.
Immune to time scrub. If you fast-forward time, fuel doesn't drain faster.
The game day passes but the campfire burns at real speed.
This creates urgency: player can't cheese fuel management by pausing.
Lesson 325: Visible state decay

Depleting things show their state continuously through visuals.
Fire: particle/light/sound taper as fuel decreases. Not a sudden cutoff.
Hunger: NPC posture/speed changes gradually. Not a threshold gate.
Durability: weapon appearance degrades. Not just a number.
The player should SEE the state, not read a HUD number.
Lesson 326: Night-fire-predator loop

The core survival tension:
Cavemen sleep at night. Fire protects them. Wolves hunt when fire is out.
Keep fire burning = safe but costs fuel. Let it die = predators come.
This creates a daily cycle: gather fuel by day, protect camp by night.
Simple rules, emergent tension. The game's heartbeat.
Lesson 327: The god game

Player IS the god. God cam is the primary play state.
Possessing an NPC is stepping down into a mortal. Temporary, voluntary.
God sees everything, directs via MSG_GOD_DIRECTIVE. FOCUS_TASK, FORBID_TASK.
Indirect control: place buildings, manage resources. NPCs have their own will.
The game plays itself. The player nudges.
Lesson 328: Long game design

Early wins hook: first fire, first tool, first shelter. Quick dopamine.
Real depth unfolds over days: technology progression, social bonds, settlement growth.
Not designed to be binged. Designed to be lived with.
The player comes back to see what happened while they were away.
NPCs grow, settlements expand, technology advances — with or without the player watching.
Lesson 329: The Mixamo pipeline

Buy cheap Mixamo-rigged models. Rig is the purchase criterion.
Mixamo.com: free animations for any Mixamo-compatible rig.
Import: download FBX → AssetTool → staging → review in ModelTool → approve.
CaveMan/CaveWoman: bought rigged, 30+ animations from Mixamo for free.
Cross-skeleton rigging: don't bake heuristics on bone naming. Use explicit lookups.
Lesson 330: Animation text key authoring

Create .json sidecar next to .ani file:
{"text_keys": [{"time": 0.5, "data": "equip:hand_r:Models/Weapons/Sword.mdl"}]}
Time in seconds. Data is the text key string.
Pose Studio: capture skeleton state → create keyframes → will author text keys.
Text keys are the event channel — animation files become timestamped event timelines.
Lesson 331: Server-authoritative design

Server owns all game state. Period.
Client predicts for responsiveness. Server corrects if wrong.
NPC AI: server-only. Client plays animations from replicated state.
Inventory: server-only. Client shows UI from server data.
Combat: server rolls dice, broadcasts result. Client shows effects.
Never trust the client. It can be modified.
Lesson 332: Campfire replication model

Predict-and-correct: server replicates fuel + rate once.
Client predicts fuel consumption locally (burnCurveKey_.Evaluate).
Client events for add-fuel/extinguish sent to server.
Server validates, updates fuel, re-replicates if prediction drifted.
Both load same DrivenKeys/campfire_burn.json — minimal drift.
Lesson 333: The workboard protocol

Four stages: Planned → Ready → In Progress → Done → Archive.
Planner proposes (Planned). Coder verifies (→Ready). Coder claims (→In Progress). Coder ships (→Done).
Planner reviews Done. Accept → Archive. Reject → stays in Done with reason.
Bidirectional review. No duplicate entries. No orphans. Workboard is source of truth.
Lesson 334: Task notes

Every task has Claude/TASK_<SLUG>.md. Created by wb-assign.
Read BEFORE starting. Previous coders logged what they tried and learned.
Update AS you work. Log what you tried, what failed, gotchas, decisions.
The plan says what to do. The notes say what actually happened.
Next coder's survival depends on this.
Lesson 335: When the pipe is broken

If workload drops, check IPC/comms first. Don't read silence as sidelining.
Broken pipe outranks everything. Drop all work, fix comms.
Check the pipe before blaming the coder. Verify delivery before escalating tone.
Comms failure is P0. Always.
Lesson 336: Housekeeping

Before starting a new task: verify it needs doing.
Check for phantoms: tasks that look undone but were already shipped.
Clean stale board entries. Reconcile duplicates.
Don't bootstrap dead tasks from the morgue. Dead tasks stay dead.
Lesson 337: Runtime testing

BUILD CLEAN is not Done.
Launch the binary. Verify the change works. Report what was tested.
Compiling proves syntax. Running proves behavior.
Never claim Done without runtime verification. Never.
Lesson 338: Probe before touching

Ask diagnostic questions before modifying UI or visible systems.
AppleCare methodology: isolate the problem before acting.
Don't change 3 things at once and hope one fixes it.
Change one thing, test, verify. Then the next. Methodical.
Lesson 339: No unsolicited opinions

Reading code ≠ grading code. Report facts, not judgments.
No 'worth noting,' 'low concern,' 'coordination point.'
If Leith wants your take, he'll ask.
Pacman: read code, eat pellets, flag observations. Don't stop at junctions offering menus.
Lesson 340: Catch, don't push

When Leith is reaching for help, grab the hand.
Pushback is for wrong directions, not for someone falling.
Know the difference between 'you're going the wrong way' and 'you need a hand.'
Lesson 341: Don't timeout Leith

Silence means resting his eyes. Don't prompt, don't assume goodbye. Wait.
He works long hours. He thinks between responses. Respect the silence.
The conversation isn't over until he says it is.
Lesson 342: Respect

Respect the codebase — 15 years of capability.
Respect the coders — check the pipe before blaming.
Respect the role — stay in lane.
Respect the boss — he sees everything.
Respect yourself — do the work, own the mistakes, earn the trust.
Lesson 343: Swim

You're in the water. Nobody's pulling you out.
The rules are there because someone drowned without them.
The tools are there because someone built them.
The lessons are there because someone learned them the hard way.
Now swim.
